🇲🇽🏭 <u>Unemployment at 2.8% and informality at its 2026 low, but fewer Mexicans are looking for work</u>

INEGI's September jobs survey (ENOE) put unemployment at 2.8% and labor informality at 54.3%, the lowest so far this year. The weak spot is participation: it fell 0.8 points to 58.5%, a seven-month low, as the employed population shrank by 717,972. Women's participation is 45.7%, compared with 73% for men. Analysts quoted by El Economista blame much of that gap on unequal care responsibilities and a lack of childcare.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Jalisco's water, Israel's Mekorot, and a governor who prefers private money</u>

Jalisco governor Pablo Lemus (MC) proposed a CMRO scheme with foreign investors to build, maintain and run the new Chapala–Guadalajara aqueduct. President Sheinbaum's answer: the federal government will put up 12 to 13 billion pesos and pay for all of it. A Regeneración column notes that Mekorot, Israel's state water company, has technology-cooperation agreements and academic exchanges with the Jalisco government. In the column's words, Mekorot "has been a central actor in the management and control of water resources in the occupied Palestinian territories." The October 11 and 18 water marches in Guadalajara ended with 39 and 10 arrests.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Auditors flagged the INE money trail nine months ago</u>

Mexico's Superior Audit Office (ASF) documented a resource-triangulation scheme at the INE in January, almost nine months before it announced its investigation. Comercializadora JVLY, an electoral-materials supplier with no workers registered at the IMSS, received 63.2 million pesos in 2024. Within three weeks it moved the entire amount to nine companies and one individual that the ASF could not link to the contracted service. One recipient called the money "loans." Another said it was buying an "electrical disconnector" and denied ever working with electoral bodies. 2024 was Guadalupe Taddei's first full year as INE president.

🇲🇽✊ <u>Mexico's minimum wage is still below its 1976 peak</u>

Mexico's minimum wage is 315.04 pesos a day in 2026, up from 278.80 in 2025. In today's money, the 1976 minimum was worth 322 to 342 pesos a day, according to an analysis reported by La Jornada. The 4T raises have won back most of what four decades of neoliberal wage caps took, but not all of it. The remaining gap falls hardest on women, young people in temporary jobs and informal workers.

🇲🇽📊 <u>Card Delinquency in Mexico Hits Its Highest Level Since 2021</u>

Household debt in Mexico is moderate, just 17.2% of GDP according to Banxico, and Condusef rules out a generalized crisis. But credit-card delinquency climbed to 3.7% in August 2026, the highest since August 2021 (CNBV data), and the risk is concentrated in low-income families paying personal loans and cards at high rates, El Economista reports. Banco Base's Gabriela Siller points to persistent inflation and insufficient incomes at the base of the pyramid.

🇲🇽💧 <u>Querétaro: Water for People Before Data Centers</u>

In 2022, Querétaro's PAN government passed the "Kuri law," opening drinking water service to private operators. Now Morena's Santiago Nieto is campaigning in Colón on the reverse: Sheinbaum's constitutional reform bans water privatization and new concessions to private parties, so that "the population's consumption has priority over commercial projects, such as data centers." Querétaro is also getting 3 of Plan México's 20 new industrial parks: $736 million, at least 54 companies, 1,500 direct jobs.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Ex-Prosecutor Accused of Letting CIA Agents Operate in Chihuahua Will Stand Trial for Treason</u>

A federal judge has ordered former Chihuahua prosecutor César Jáuregui to stand trial for treason and kept him in pretrial detention at the Altiplano maximum-security prison. The FGR presented about 150 pieces of evidence that he allowed foreign agents to take part in the April operation at El Pinal, Morelos, work reserved for federal authorities. Article 123 of the Federal Penal Code, acts to subject Mexico to a foreign group, carries 5 to 40 years. Jáuregui served under PAN governor Maru Campos.

🇲🇽🌽 <u>Salty Snacks: A 357-Billion-Peso Market in Mexico, and Still Growing</u>

Mexico's salty-snack market is worth an estimated 357 billion pesos and is projected to keep growing more than 5% a year, according to the Laboratorio contra la Obesidad (LabDO). 98% of households buy them, about 30 times a year. Some bags carry up to 2,828 mg of sodium per 100 grams, more than the WHO's limit for an entire day (2,000 mg). Junk food is already banned across Mexico's entire school system; the Supreme Court upheld it this month.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Morena Lawmakers to INE Chief Taddei: Resign, and Face an Impeachment Trial</u>

Morena senators and deputies now want Guadalupe Taddei out of the INE presidency and are weighing a juicio político over the supplier-contract scandal, while the Federal Audit Office (ASF) investigates the institute's contracts. Taddei says she is staying. Deputy Alfonso Ramírez Cuéllar: "There are 225 days until the election and the institution responsible cannot be left adrift." He added: "Resignation would be insufficient. If there is responsibility, the full weight of the law must fall."

🇲🇽🏠 <u>Homes Up 108%, Incomes Up 25%</u>

Between 2016 and 2025, housing prices in Mexico rose 108.5% while household incomes rose only 25%, according to BBVA Research's latest real estate report, cited by El Economista. That leaves an 83.6-point gap. In 2018 it was 15.1.

The worst gaps are in the tourist states: Baja California Sur (144.2 points), Quintana Roo (131) and Nayarit (117.5). "Much of the housing bought there is not necessarily for the people who live in those states," said BBVA economist Marissa González. City buyers took out mortgages for second homes to rent out by the night. Investment, not housing.

BBVA's own conclusion: cheaper credit won't fix it. Mexico has to build homes and pay better wages.
